chapter.title: The Prop Drilling Problem
chapter.description: What context is for, and the cheaper fixes worth trying first.

blocks.text: Props flow down one level at a time. When a value is needed five levels deep, every component in between has to accept it and pass it on, even though none of them use it. That is **prop drilling**.

blocks.code:
<App theme={theme}>
  <Layout theme={theme}>
    <Sidebar theme={theme}>
      <Nav theme={theme}>
        <NavButton theme={theme} />   {/* finally used here */}

blocks.text: It is not just ugly. Every intermediate component now has a prop it must keep in its type definition, and renaming the value means touching all of them.
Prop drilling often disappears if you pass the finished element instead of the data. The component that owns the data creates the child, so nothing in between needs to know.
Reach for composition before context. It keeps data flow explicit and does not add a new indirection to trace when you are debugging.

items: Values genuinely needed everywhere: theme, locale, the current user, feature flags.
Values that change rarely, so re-render cost is low.
Compound components where a parent must talk to distant children, such as tabs or accordions.

blocks.text: Context is not a state manager. It is a way to deliver a value down the tree. Frequently changing data in a widely used context re-renders large parts of your app.

blocks.text: A context is created once at module level, provided somewhere near the top of the tree, and read anywhere below.
The argument to `createContext` is used only when a component reads the context with no matching provider above it. It is a fallback, not an initial value.
A missing provider is a common bug and a silent one - the component quietly gets the default. Guard against it in your custom hook.
Wrapping the provider in a hook
Exporting a `useTheme` hook rather than the raw context gives you one place to add validation, defaults or logging later, and stops the context object leaking across your codebase.
A component reads the nearest provider above it, so nesting lets a subtree override the value.
